bib.title: Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 2016 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pages 1317-1327

question: Can knowledge distillation, including new sequence-level variants, compress large NMT models into small fast students with little loss in BLEU?
hypothesis: Training the student on the teacher's beam-search outputs (its approximate sequence mode) transfers sequence-level knowledge and removes the need for beam search at test time.
contributions: Apply word-level knowledge distillation to NMT
Introduce sequence-level knowledge distillation (Seq-KD) and sequence-level interpolation (Seq-Inter)
Show students run 10x faster than teacher with beam search with little BLEU loss
Combine with weight pruning for 13x fewer parameters at -0.4 BLEU

method.summary: Teacher NMT (attentional LSTM seq2seq, Luong 2015) is trained on gold data; beam search over the training set yields new targets (Seq-KD) or the beam hypothesis with highest smoothed sentence BLEU against gold (Seq-Inter); a smaller student is trained with ordinary NLL on those targets, optionally with word-level KD loss, and optionally pruned by magnitude then retrained.

datasets.name: WMT 2014 English-German
datasets.preprocessing: top 50k most frequent words kept, rest replaced with UNK; Seq-Inter data generated on ~50% of the training set for efficiency

models.name: Teacher 4x1000 LSTM (En-De)
models.architecture: LSTM seq2seq with global-general attention and input feeding (Luong et al. 2015)

training.objective: NLL on teacher beam outputs (Seq-KD); mixture (1-alpha)*NLL + alpha*cross-entropy to teacher word distribution (Word-KD); NLL on highest-BLEU beam hypothesis (Seq-Inter)
training.lr: 0.1 for Seq-Inter fine-tuning; 0.2 for retraining pruned model on Seq-KD data then 0.1 for Seq-Inter fine-tune

other.other_details: Other training details mirror Luong et al. (2015), not restated
other.seq_inter_init: fine-tune from pretrained model (original data or Seq-KD data)
other.pruning: remove weights with lowest absolute value, retrain

inference.decoding: greedy (K=1) and beam search K=5 for evaluation; teacher data generation beam K=5 for Seq-KD, K=35 for Seq-Inter
inference.samples: single run per config; no seeds reported

other.speed_hardware: GeForce GTX Titan X GPU, CPU (unspecified), Samsung Galaxy 6 smartphone

metrics.name: BLEU
metrics.definition: tokenized BLEU with multi-bleu.perl, greedy (K=1) and beam 5

metrics.name: p(t=y_hat)
metrics.definition: probability of greedy-decoded output sequence, averaged over test set

metrics.name: Decoding speed
metrics.definition: average source words translated per second

baselines: same-size student trained on original data
eval.protocol: Single reported value per cell; no seeds, no significance tests.

limits: Only two language pairs and LSTM attention models; no Transformers.
Single run per cell, no seeds or significance reported.
Optimizer, batch size, epochs, dropout and hardware for training are not stated (deferred to Luong et al. 2015).
Seq-KD student has much higher perplexity (22.7 vs 8.2) and is more peaked.
Speed benchmarks: CPU model unspecified; 4x1000 teacher could not run on smartphone.
Authors note Seq-KD approximates teacher distribution with a single beam mode that holds only ~1-3% of mass.

terms.definition: Student is trained on the teacher-generated data, which is the result of running beam search and taking the highest-scoring sequence with the teacher model.
Student is trained on the sequence on the teacher's beam that had the highest BLEU against gold.
